title: Any bug in a deployed contract is treated as proof that quality control failed, not that an individual erred
content:
A.1.10.2.4.7.4.2 grounds line-by-line review in the irreversibility of the artifact: "Sky Core Contracts are immutable, and disabling them often requires waiting for a long period. As such, bugs and exploits should never be present in production code." Then it makes an attribution claim: **"Any deployed contract that contains a bug indicates that the existing quality control, auditing, and review processes are not adequately preventing bugs."**

That sentence relocates blame by default. A production bug is not evidence that a developer was careless — it is evidence that the system which is supposed to catch careless developers did not. Individual error is assumed to be constant and inevitable; the controls are the variable.

A.1.10.2.4.7.3.6 operationalizes this in the retrospective, which must document "any measures that were **previously in place** to prevent this type of issue occurring, and any measures that can be implemented going forward." The first half is the hard question: something was supposed to catch this, and naming it forces the analysis past "be more careful" toward a specific control that was missing, misapplied or unenforced.

The practical benefit is honest reporting. When a bug indicts the process rather than the person, the discoverer — often the author — has far less reason to minimize it, which is what makes the surrounding detection and classification machinery actually get used. The same claim also sets a demanding standard: it implies the review process must be improvable after every single defect, with no category of bug written off as unavoidable.
description: A.1.10.2.4.7.4.2 attributes production bugs to inadequate review and auditing processes, and A.1.10.2.4.7.3.6 requires retrospectives to name the control that was supposed to catch it.
